content: When one object exerts a force on another, the second object exerts an equal and opposite force back onto the first object. A classic example of this phenomenon is observed when two ice skaters push against each other, causing them to slide apart in opposite directions. Another example is the recoil of a firearm, where the force propelling the bullet forward is matched by an equal force pushing the gun backward, which is felt by the shooter. The resulting accelerations of the two objects can differ due to differences in their masses, as seen in the case of firearm recoil. A well-known anecdote suggests that Isaac Newton was inspired to develop his theory of universal gravitation after observing an apple fall from a tree. Popular depictions, such as cartoons, have exaggerated this story, claiming the apple struck Newton on the head, leading to his realization of gravity. John Conduitt, Newton's assistant at the Royal Mint and the husband of Newton's niece, documented the event, noting that Newton's inquiry was not about the existence of gravity but whether it extended far enough from Earth to also govern the Moon's orbit. Newton demonstrated that if the gravitational force decreased with the square of the distance, it could accurately predict the Moon's orbital period. This insight led him to hypothesize that the same force was responsible for other orbital motions, which he termed universal gravitation. William Stukeley, a contemporary of Newton, recorded a conversation in 1726 where Newton recalled the moment the concept of gravitation first occurred to him. He described sitting in contemplation and observing an apple fall, prompting him to wonder why the apple always descended perpendicularly to the ground rather than moving sideways or upwards. Similarly, Voltaire wrote in 1727 that Newton conceived his system of gravitation while walking in his garden and observing a falling apple. These accounts are likely embellishments of Newton's own story about watching an apple fall from a tree while sitting by a window at his home, Woolsthorpe Manor. There are various claims regarding the identity of the specific apple tree Newton observed. The King’s School in Grantham asserts that the tree was later uprooted and moved to the headmaster’s garden, while the staff at Woolsthorpe Manor, now owned by the National Trust, argue that a tree in their garden is the one described by Newton. A descendant of the original tree can be seen outside the main gate of Trinity College, Cambridge, near the room where Newton lived during his studies. The National Fruit Collection at Brogdale offers grafts from a tree resembling the Flower of Kent, a coarse-fleshed cooking apple variety, which is believed to be the same type as Newton’s tree. Newton’s writings include significant works such as Method of Fluxions (1671), De Motu Corporum in Gyrum (1684), and the groundbreaking Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica (1687). Other notable publications include Opticks (1704), Arithmetica Universalis (1707), and posthumous works like The System of the World and Observations on Daniel and The Apocalypse of St. John. His contributions extended beyond science, as seen in his reports as Master of the Mint (1701–1725) and his historical and theological writings. French mathematician Joseph-Louis Lagrange regarded Newton as the greatest genius who ever lived, remarking that Newton was also the most fortunate, as the opportunity to establish a system of the world arises only once. English poet Alexander Pope famously commemorated Newton’s achievements with the epitaph: Nature and Nature’s laws lay hid in night; God said, ‘Let Newton be.’ and all was light. Despite such praise, Newton was modest about his accomplishments, though his modesty has been debated. In a 1676 letter to Robert Hooke, Newton wrote, If I have seen further, it is by standing on the shoulders of giants. Historians often interpret this as a veiled critique of Hooke, with whom Newton had disputes over optical discoveries, rather than a simple expression of humility. This interpretation aligns with Newton’s contentious relationships regarding his discoveries, such as the priority dispute over the invention of calculus. In popular culture, Newton is a central figure in Neal Stephenson’s The Baroque Cycle, a series of novels exploring the emergence of modern science. Newton’s work in the Principia, his interest in alchemy, and his disputes over calculus are key plot points. The novels also depict a fictional metaphysical debate between Newton and Gottfried Leibniz, moderated by Caroline of Ansbach. Additionally, the development of a moneyand credit-based economy is a major theme, with Newton’s tenure at the Royal Mint and his efforts against counterfeiters culminating in the Trial of the Pyx.
